issues.legal_issue: A revenue officer considering objections to a draft record of rights may determine the correctness of an entry describing a person’s status when that status has been challenged in the objection.
material_facts: The published draft record described the appellant as a raiyat.
The respondent amended his objection to seek entry of the appellant as a tenure holder and himself as a lessee under the appellant.
The appellant consented to the amendment, and the revenue officer considered and decided the challenge to the appellant’s status.
The government had not separately challenged the appellant’s status.
issues.conclusion: The revenue officer had jurisdiction to decide the objection to the appellant’s recorded status, and the challenge to the entry recording him as a tenure holder failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 44(1) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 authorizes a Revenue Officer to receive and consider objections to any entry in a draft record of rights. An objection challenging the description of a person’s status falls within that authority; the government’s failure to object does not deprive the officer of jurisdiction.

predicates.draft_record_objection_proceeding: A proceeding was brought to consider an objection to an entry in a draft record of rights.
predicates.status_entry_challenged: An objector challenged the recorded status of a person in the draft record.

issues.definition: When an objection proceeding concerns a draft record and an objector challenges a person’s recorded status, the revenue officer may decide that status entry.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction may not overturn concurrent factual findings of revenue tribunals merely because it would assess the evidence differently.
material_facts: The Settlement Officer and the appellate District Judge both found that the respondent was a temporary lessee.

The respondent’s possession was undisputed, and evidence included the appellant’s failure to produce accounts, an admitted payment described as an advance, and a compromise concerning the respondent’s possession and departure.
The High Court reappraised the evidence and set aside the finding of a temporary lease.
The Supreme Court found that the revenue authorities’ conclusion had evidentiary material supporting it and was not shown to be perverse or beyond their jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the concurrent finding that the respondent was a temporary lessee; the appeal challenging that interference was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution confers supervisory, not appellate, jurisdiction. Under Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner, Hills Division, Assam, [1958] S.C.R. 1240, the High Court may intervene to keep subordinate tribunals within their authority, including where findings are based on no material or are perverse, but may not correct ordinary errors in appreciating evidence. Here, the evidence provided material supporting the revenue tribunals’ finding.

rule.if: supervisory_jurisdiction_proceeding and concurrent_tribunal_findings and supporting_material_exists and not jurisdictional_overreach and not perverse_finding

predicates.supervisory_jurisdiction_proceeding: A party brought the tribunal’s decision before a High Court in a proceeding exercising supervisory rather than appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_tribunal_findings: The first-instance tribunal and the tribunal hearing the appeal reached the same factual finding.
predicates.supporting_material_exists: Evidence before the tribunals provided a basis for the factual finding.
predicates.jurisdictional_overreach: The tribunals exceeded the limits of their authority in reaching the finding.
predicates.perverse_finding: The finding was perverse, including because it was based on no material.

issues.definition: When a supervisory proceeding challenges concurrent tribunal findings supported by material, and the tribunals neither exceeded their authority nor made a perverse finding, the High Court must not set those findings aside.

issues.legal_issue: A revenue officer conducting an inquiry that is subject to a statutory appeal must maintain a record of oral evidence sufficient to preserve the effectiveness of that appeal.
material_facts: The parties adduced oral evidence before the Settlement Officer.
The officer made no record of that evidence, leaving the appellate authority unable to ascertain precisely what the witnesses had said except where the order referred to it.
An appeal from the officer’s order was available on factual and legal questions.
The applicable rules did not expressly require a record of oral evidence.
issues.conclusion: Even though no specific rule required it, the Settlement Officer was required to maintain some record of the oral evidence so that the statutory appeal would remain an effective remedy; he was not required to follow the procedure for recording evidence in civil courts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 44(3) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 provides an appeal from an order on an objection under section 44(1). The right of appeal is intended to afford full relief and would be ineffective if the appellate authority could not ascertain the material before the first-instance officer. The requirement to maintain some record of oral evidence is implicit in the statutory appeal provision, even where the rules do not expressly impose it.

predicates.objection_inquiry_with_statutory_appeal: An officer decided an objection in an inquiry whose decision was subject to a statutory appeal.
predicates.oral_evidence_received: Witnesses gave oral evidence before the officer.

issues.definition: When an officer receives oral evidence in an objection inquiry subject to a statutory appeal, the officer must keep a record sufficient for the appeal to be effective.
